Question: The ancient masters who established [the system] all spoke of three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
why does Dignāga now state that there are only two?

first, the specific (svalakṣaṇa), and second, the general (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
A mind that apprehends its own specific characteristic is called direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The mind that apprehends common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is called inference (*anumāna*).
When the concentrated mind takes the teaching as its object,
it immediately attains the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When the distracted mind takes the teaching as its object, it immediately apprehends the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

The *Yìzuǎnyào yǒujì* on the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* states: "The master of the compilation was originally named Huìxuán; out of deference to the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang], he changed his name to Huìzhǎo," and so forth.

Completed on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the second year of Shōji (the Gengshen year), written by Shinsei at the eastern annex of Chōshō-ji; this is based on the colophon of the original manuscript.
The *Hon’oki* states:

"The śramaṇa Zuishun of Kōfuku-ji respectfully made a vow to transcribe all the sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and commentaries of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; following his exhortation, Kakuen of the same temple completed the transcription."
At that time, on the eighth day of the eighth month of the fourth year of Jōan, in the year of Wuchen (1188), the Great Dharma Master Zō transmitted [the text];
subsequently, Kōkei, who was commissioned to transcribe it, respectfully completed the transcription and proofreading.
Recorded on the twenty-ninth day of the first month of spring in the second year of Eiman.
The colophon at the end of the punctuated manuscript states: "Minshun of Gengō briefly completed the collation in the eighth year of Tenjō."

On the twenty-sixth day of the third month in the ninth year, [I] lectured at Kōfuku-ji. The monk Jōjaku stated that on the final day of the second month in the year of Gengo (the thirty-seventh year of the Anwa era), he had borrowed this book from the Sōjū Myōsen, who had made annotations upon it, and so forth.
Written on the twenty-first day of the eighth month in the second year of Jiaying, the Gengyin year, by the scribe-monk Chenghui; the inner text was completed on the second day of the ninth month.
It was written under the lamp at the hour of Hai on the same year, month, and day.
It was finalized under the lamp at approximately the hour of Xu on the thirteenth day of the same ninth month.

During the four days of the twentieth, twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-third of that same month, while adding my own humble observations to the collation, various external circumstances intervened, causing the progress of the work to be slow. Within this period, I devoted myself exclusively to ritual ablutions and donned my dharma robes; as for the copying of this single volume of thirty-eight sheets and the addition of the punctuation marks, I requested the monk Jōe to complete the task. Thus, the merit of the collation belongs solely to this humble monk. By means of these roots of goodness, I respectfully repay the four debts of gratitude, so that this humble monk may emerge from the mire of birth and death, and all sentient beings may swiftly ascend to the other shore of Bodhi.

Recorded by the junior scholar-monk Śramaṇa Jue Xian during the sixth month of summer in the second year of the Zhengzhi era. The transcription was completed at the Shichao Sheng Temple by the monk Xin Xi at the Shilang Room. This copy was obtained by Yongzun from the library of Master Deye.

On the third day of the first ten days of the seventh month of that same year, I moved the reading marks (*doku*) and completed the transcription. This work was transcribed at Hōshaku-in; indeed, it was during a time when the world suffered from famine and human strength had declined, yet I persevered in the task of transcription with diligent effort to sustain my life. My aspiration in undertaking this was twofold: first, that the construction of the temple’s *garan* may be swiftly completed and the Buddha-Dharma may flourish, while my own life may be long and sustained; second, that upon rebirth in the Inner Court (*naikai*), I may behold the Compassionate Honored One face-to-face, never retreat in mind, and attain Bodhi.
